method: Manually curated, source-scoped relationships. A link can be a directly cited edited line, an object-level catalogue association, a related research route, or a distinct biblical textual comparison; it is never automatically claimed to be the same historical event or person. No name-identity resolution, epigraphic authentication, or biblical-archaeological harmonisation is inferred from lexical similarity.

terms.label: Aššur
terms.description: The city recorded as the findspot of several Middle Assyrian administrative objects; distinguish a documented excavation location from the wider biblical name Asshur.

objects.note: KAJ 247 is catalogued from the M 09 archive at Aššur; this is an archaeological findspot association.
KAJ 233 is catalogued from Aššur, also in the M 09 archive.
KAJ 118 has an Aššur archive excavation label.

passages.note: Genesis refers to Asshur and cities in a different ancient literary setting; this is not an archaeological findspot record.

terms.label: Šibaniba (Tell Billa)
terms.description: A named provincial archive site, securely distinguished from the capital and its differently organised administrative records.

objects.note: Billa 30 is attributed to the Aššur-kašid archive at Šibaniba.

terms.label: Nineveh
terms.description: The Assyrian centre named in biblical prophecy and in a later Babylonian chronicle, with separate copy and event dates.

objects.note: The chronicle refers to the fall of Nineveh; its surviving physical copy was made later.

passages.note: Nahum opens with a prophetic oracle concerning Nineveh, not a military diary.
Zephaniah includes a prophetic statement concerning Assyria and Nineveh.

terms.label: Palace administration
terms.description: Official records describe how goods and personnel were assigned through palace offices, not a complete economic census.

objects.note: The straw opening connects a commodity quantity to a palace administrative receipt.
This palace document records footwear and an individual identified by a status term.
The provincial account associates barley and palace obligations.

terms.label: Temple setting
terms.description: A cuneiform text identifies an institutional temple context while leaving the personal beliefs of its listed participants unrecorded.

objects.note: The edited line includes a temple logogram.

terms.label: Barley
terms.description: Barley appears in several separate Middle Assyrian administrative receipts; their different dates and people must not be collapsed into one event.

objects.note: Barley is expressed with ancient capacity signs in this single horse-provisioning record.
The opening quantity belongs to a city-guard provision account.
A provincial receipt records a separate barley quantity.

terms.label: Straw
terms.description: A specific record of palace straw, not proof of region-wide agricultural yields or delivery outcomes.

objects.note: The edition records forty sacks associated with straw.

terms.label: Lead
terms.description: An ancient measure of lead is linked to a house-related obligation; no modern valuation is inferred.

objects.note: The tablet begins a legal-economic statement with a lead measure.

terms.label: Service horse
terms.description: A documented equine barley provision, not a count of the cavalry or a reconstruction of a horse's diet.

objects.note: The associated passage concerns barley supplied for a service horse.

terms.label: Palace footwear
terms.description: A recorded pair of shoes illustrates administrative distribution and its limits when used to reconstruct an individual's story.

objects.note: The receipt concerns footwear from a palace context.

terms.label: Guard provisioning
terms.description: A ten-day allocation lists different guard groups, without documenting actual food consumption or an annual ration.

objects.note: The published line refers to a ten-day allocation.

terms.label: House transaction
terms.description: A house sale and lead obligation are connected in a particular tablet; ownership history and the result remain unknown.

objects.note: The published obverse clause refers to a house sale, but its later legal outcome is not established.

terms.label: Seal impressions
terms.description: A physical tablet has two cylinder-seal impressions, while other edited receipts contain seal notation; no unverified identity is supplied.

objects.note: The Met catalogues two cylinder-seal impressions, without a verified line edition.
This receipt includes a seal notation, without identifying a new signer here.

terms.label: Workers in accounts
terms.description: Institutional lists record labour or guard categories; a single label does not establish freedom, remuneration or personal identity.

objects.note: The editor qualifies the term used for the twenty-two people.
The separate guard allocation names several personnel groups.

terms.label: Hostage status
terms.description: One edited Middle Assyrian footwear record labels a recipient with a status term; it does not reveal the person's full circumstances.

objects.note: The linked edition describes the recipient as a hostage.

terms.label: Niri-šaldi
terms.description: A personal name appears in a specific damaged tablet line; no biography or unverified identity is inferred.

objects.note: The edition gives the recipient's name, partly affected by damage.

terms.label: Eponym dating
terms.description: Middle Assyrian dates can include an eponym and month/day formula; absolute BCE conversion requires separate chronology.

objects.note: A month and day appear beside a following eponym name.
The case records an eponym date elsewhere in the tablet.
The eponym marker is explicitly restored in the edition.

terms.label: Damaged and restored signs
terms.description: Brackets, damaged-sign marks and unidentified signs preserve the limits of an editor's reading.

objects.note: Square brackets identify a restored marker, not intact signs.
The editor leaves a name partly lost or unreadable.
The excerpt preserves lacunae instead of reconstructing missing words.

terms.label: Queried reading
terms.description: A scholarly question mark records uncertainty in a sign or interpretation; it is not a verified alternative translation.

objects.note: The edited phrase carries a query mark signalling that the particular sign reading remains uncertain.
The journey or campaign wording remains editorially uncertain.

terms.label: Asshur in Genesis
terms.description: A biblical place and ancestry reference used as a textual comparison, not a dated thirteenth-century administrative tablet.

passages.note: Genesis provides the primary biblical wording about Asshur and named cities; historical geography is a separate inquiry.
Genesis also lists Asshur in a genealogy; the text does not supply Middle Assyrian archive dates.

terms.label: Jehu of Israel
terms.description: A named king in 2 Kings and a subject of an Assyrian royal monument; not recorded on any of the nine Middle Assyrian tablets.

passages.note: The biblical accession account is primary for its own narrative; the Black Obelisk independently refers to tribute.

terms.label: Sargon II
terms.description: A king named in Isaiah's account of Ashdod; a later Neo-Assyrian ruler, not a Middle Assyrian administrative participant.

passages.note: Isaiah 20 describes the king and Ashdod as part of a prophetic account.

terms.label: Hezekiah of Judah
terms.description: Biblical ruler compared with Sennacherib's annals; do not substitute Middle Assyrian receipt tablets as evidence for his reign.

passages.note: Kings narrates Judah's conflict with Assyria; interpretation requires comparison with separately dated sources.

terms.label: Samaria
terms.description: A biblical account of the later Assyrian crisis and deportations, not a reference to the Middle Assyrian city guard receipts.

passages.note: Kings describes Shalmaneser, Hoshea and Samaria in the northern kingdom's crisis.
Kings separately describes later population resettlement.

terms.label: Deportation and resettlement
terms.description: An important later Neo-Assyrian biblical and historical topic that must not be conflated with a Middle Assyrian hostage or work allocation.

passages.note: The biblical text names deportation destinations following Samaria's fall.
